tests.label: Fisher's infinitesimal model of quantitative inheritance
tests.hypothesis: If adult height is governed by many Mendelian loci of small additive effect, then (a) a child's height given the parents' heights is approximately Gaussian with a residual variance (segregation plus environment) that does not depend on the parental mean, and (b) full siblings are correlated at least as strongly as parent and offspring, because dominance and shared environment add to the sibling covariance but not to the parent-offspring covariance.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: Galton's 1886 family height records as distributed in the R HistData package (GaltonFamilies: 934 adult children in 205 families with father, mother and child heights in inches and child sex). Female child heights are multiplied by 1.08, as Galton did, to put both sexes on a common scale; mid-parent height is (father + 1.08*mother)/2. Residuals r are taken from the ordinary-least-squares regression of adjusted child height on mid-parent height. Criterion A (homoscedasticity): Levene's test (median-centred, Brown-Forsythe) of residual variance across the three mid-parent terciles gives p > 0.05 AND the ratio of the largest to the smallest tercile residual variance is < 1.5. Criterion B (normality): residual sample skewness |g1| < 0.5 and excess kurtosis |g2| < 1.0. Criterion C (sibling vs parent-offspring): the full-sibling intraclass correlation of adjusted height (one-way random-effects ANOVA estimator over families with >= 2 children) is >= r_po - 0.05, where r_po is the single-parent-offspring correlation implied by the child-on-mid-parent correlation r_mp as r_po = r_mp / sqrt(2) (which assumes uncorrelated parents). SUPPORTS if A, B and C all hold.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if A fails strongly (variance ratio > 2 or Levene p < 0.001) OR B fails strongly (|g1| > 1 or |g2| > 2) OR the sibling correlation is more than 0.15 below r_po. MIXED otherwise. INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the file cannot be downloaded.
tests.interpretation: Fisher (1918) derived the covariances between relatives from Mendelian inheritance at many loci and showed they reproduce the biometric correlations; Galton's and Pearson's height data were among the biometric facts he reconciled, so this is an in-sample test of the model's distributional predictions on classic data, not an out-of-sample test. Environmental variance cannot be separated here, so criterion A tests the joint prediction that neither segregation variance nor environmental variance depends on the parental mean. Assortative mating (positive parent-parent correlation) inflates r_mp relative to sqrt(2)*r_po and so makes criterion C harder, not easier, to pass. Galton's 1.08 female adjustment is applied because the dataset is the raw one.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the CSV. analysis.py multiplies female child and mother heights by 1.08 (Galton's adjustment), forms mid-parent height, regresses adjusted child height on it, and tests the residuals: Brown-Forsythe Levene test and variance ratio across mid-parent terciles (A), sample skewness and excess kurtosis (B), and the one-way ANOVA intraclass correlation of siblings against the single-parent correlation implied by the mid-parent correlation (C). The pre-registered rule is applied.

measured.unit: ratio of largest to smallest residual variance across mid-parent terciles (model predicts 1)
measured.n: 934 children in 205 families (172 families with 2+ children)

caveats: In-sample classic data: Fisher (1918) built the model to explain exactly these biometric regularities, so the test shows the model's distributional predictions hold on Galton's families, not that they hold out of sample.

The sibling correlation (0.39) exceeds the implied parent-offspring correlation (0.35) as predicted, but shared family environment, not only dominance, can produce that excess; the two are not separable here.
Heteroscedasticity could be masked by the modest sample (about 311 children per tercile) and by Galton's rounding of heights; the variance ratio of 1.08 is nonetheless close to 1.
Galton's 1.08 female adjustment and the assumption of uncorrelated parents (observed father-mother r = 0.10) are approximations.

datasets.name: Galton's 1886 family height records (934 adult children of 205 families), as distributed in the R package HistData (GaltonFamilies), via the Rdatasets CSV mirror
datasets.license: GPL (HistData package); the 1886 data are public domain

tests.label: Fisher's principle of equal investment in the sexes
tests.hypothesis: If parents are selected to invest equally in sons and daughters and a son costs the same as a daughter, then the primary (birth) sex ratio of human populations should be close to one male per female and should not vary widely between populations.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: United Nations World Population Prospects 2024, Demographic Indicators, medium variant CSV (WPP2024_Demographic_Indicators_Medium.csv.gz), variable SRB (sex ratio at birth, males per 100 female births), rows with LocTypeName == 'Country/Area', years 1950 to 1979 inclusive (before prenatal sex determination was widely available, so the ratio reflects biology rather than sex-selective abortion), country-years with total mid-year population >= 1 million. Criterion A (equality): the median SRB across qualifying country-years lies in [95, 105] (within 5% of equal numbers). Criterion B (uniform near-equality): at least 95% of qualifying country-years lie in [90, 110]. SUPPORTS if A and B both hold.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the median SRB lies outside [90, 110] OR fewer than 80% of qualifying country-years lie in [90, 110]. MIXED otherwise (for example a consistent small excess of one sex between 5% and 10%, with B holding). INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the file cannot be downloaded or has no SRB column.
tests.interpretation: Fisher's principle concerns investment up to the end of parental care, not numbers at birth; the birth sex ratio is the only primary-allocation quantity available for a large set of human populations, and the test treats sons and daughters as equally costly, which is the case the claim's statement singles out ('1:1 when the two cost the same'). WPP 1950-1979 values are UN estimates reconstructed from censuses and vital registration, not raw counts, and are not independent across years within a country. This is a weak test of a strong claim: it can detect gross departures from equality and strong between-population variation, not fine deviations.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the gzipped CSV (16.6 MB). analysis.py keeps rows of type Country/Area for 1950-1979 with mid-year population >= 1 million and a non-missing SRB, and computes the median, mean, SD, 5th and 95th percentiles of SRB over country-years, the fractions inside [95,105] and [90,110], and per-country means; the pre-registered rule is applied.

measured.unit: median sex ratio at birth, males per 100 females, country-years 1950-1979 (equal numbers = 100)

caveats: Verdict is 'mixed' by the pre-registered rule: every one of 4222 country-years lies within 10% of equality (criterion B, the strong-constraint prediction, holds with no exceptions), but the median is 105.2, just outside the 5% band of criterion A, and the excess of male births is systematic (minimum country mean 101.0).

The standard Fisherian reading of the 5% male excess is that boys die more often before the end of parental investment, so investment is nearer equality than births are; this test did not measure sex-specific child mortality and so cannot confirm that reconciliation.
WPP values are UN estimates reconstructed from censuses and registration systems, smoothed and not independent across years within a country; the effective sample size is far below 4222.
Only humans were tested, and only the 'equal cost' case; Fisher's principle predicts equal investment, which the birth ratio measures only approximately.

datasets.name: United Nations World Population Prospects 2024, Demographic Indicators, medium variant (CSV)

tests.label: Local mate competition sex ratio
tests.hypothesis: If mothers adjust the sex ratio of their offspring to the degree of local mate competition, then in the parasitoid wasp Nasonia vitripennis the proportion of sons should rise with the number of foundresses laying on a host, and for n >= 2 foundresses should lie near Hamilton's unbeatable value (n - 1) / (2n).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: Cook et al. (2015) 'DNA methylation and sex allocation in the parasitoid wasp Nasonia vitripennis', Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.15nj0, file DryadData.xlsx; only control (untreated or vehicle-treated) females are used, with the number of co-foundresses and the numbers of sons and daughters per brood or host as given in the file. SUPPORTS if Spearman rho(number of foundresses, proportion of sons) > 0 with p < 0.05 across broods AND the mean absolute deviation between the observed mean proportion of sons at each foundress number n >= 2 and (n - 1) / (2n) is <= 0.10.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if rho <= 0 or p >= 0.05 (no increase of the son proportion with foundress number). MIXED if the increase is present but the deviation from (n - 1) / (2n) exceeds 0.10. INCONCLUSIVE (not-operationalizable) if the file does not record foundress number per brood. INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if Dryad keeps blocking automated download (as of 2026-10-31 it serves a JavaScript proof-of-work challenge to scripted requests, which this project does not circumvent) and no manually downloaded copy with a recorded checksum is supplied.
tests.interpretation: Nasonia is haplodiploid; the claim states the diploid formula, which is used as stated. The haplodiploid correction (Hamilton 1979) raises the predicted son proportion slightly, which is noted but not applied. Single-foundress broods are excluded from the deviation criterion because the formula gives zero sons at n = 1 while a mother must produce at least one son to fertilise her daughters; they are included in the correlation.
tests.method: fetch.py requested the file(s) by their Dryad file-stream URLs with a plain HTTP client and received HTTP 403 with a proof-of-work challenge page (the Dryad API download endpoint requires an account token). Per BEST_PRACTICES.md, sites that block automated requests are not circumvented, so no data were inspected and no analysis was run. fetch.py accepts a manually downloaded copy placed in data/ and records its checksum; the pre-registered analysis can then be run without changing the criteria.
caveats: The dataset exists and is public (CC0) but could not be fetched by script; a person with a browser can download it in seconds, after which this test is runnable as pre-registered.
Dryad's metadata API (which does not require a token) confirmed the file names and sizes; nothing about the data values was seen.

datasets.name: Cook et al. (2015) 'DNA methylation and sex allocation in the parasitoid wasp Nasonia vitripennis', Dryad data (DryadData.xlsx, 33.5 KB)

tests.label: Declining force of selection with age
tests.hypothesis: If the force of selection on survival declines with age after reproduction begins so that senescence is inevitable, then in age-structured matrix population models of unmanipulated wild animal populations, age-specific mortality should rise across the adult (reproductive) age classes in the great majority of species.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: COMADRE Animal Matrix Database v4.26.4.0 (RData file served at compadre-db.org/Data/ComadreDownload; data user agreement and citation guidelines accepted). Matrix selection: MatrixCriteriaAge == 'Yes' (age-classified), MatrixSplit == 'Divided' (U and F submatrices available), MatrixComposite in {'Individual', 'Mean'}, MatrixTreatment == 'Unmanipulated', MatrixCaptivity == 'W' (wild), matrix dimension >= 5, no missing entries in U or F. For each qualifying matrix, survival of age class a is the column sum of U for class a; the last class is dropped from the trend if U has a non-zero diagonal entry there (an open-ended plus group whose survival mixes ages). Mature classes are those whose F column sum is > 0. For each species, qualifying matrices of the same dimension are averaged element-wise (so each species contributes once); species with fewer than 4 mature age classes after dropping the plus group are excluded. Rising adult mortality = Spearman rho between age-class index and mortality (1 - survival) over the mature classes is > 0. SUPPORTS if at least 80% of qualifying species show rising adult mortality AND the mean rho across species is > 0.3. AMENDMENT (2026-10-31, before any data were downloaded, at the request of the holdout thread): species of class Aves are excluded from the primary analysis and from all criteria above; bird species are held out and only reported separately, unfitted, as a holdout check. Class is taken from COMADRE's 'Class' metadata column.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if fewer than 50% of qualifying species show rising adult mortality. MIXED otherwise (50% to 80%, or >= 80% with mean rho <= 0.3). INCONCLUSIVE (underpowered) if fewer than 15 species qualify; INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the file cannot be downloaded or read.
tests.interpretation: The proved part of the claim is the formula for s(a); the biological assertion tested is that senescence (rising mortality with adult age) is the inevitable result, which is how Jones et al. (2013) tested it across the tree of life and the reason the claim is already marked refuted in the claim graph. Matrix models average over years and individuals, late age classes are estimated from few animals, and many published matrices truncate age at a plus group; these all add noise rather than a systematic sign. Age classes are the model's classes (usually years), not ages since maturity, which is adequate for a monotonic-trend test. The RData file is converted to JSON with an R script (R 4.x) because the matrices are stored as R lists; analysis.py reads the committed JSON.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the RData file and exports metadata and U, F, C submatrices to JSON with an R script (jsonlite). analysis.py keeps age-classified, divided, unmanipulated, wild, individual-or-mean matrices of dimension >= 5 with finite entries; averages a species' matrices of its most common dimension; takes survival per class as the U column sum, drops a terminal class with a self-loop (open plus group), defines mature classes by positive F column sums, and computes Spearman rho between class index and mortality over >= 4 mature classes (constant mortality counted as rho = 0). Bird species are excluded before the verdict. The pre-registered rule is applied.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying non-bird species with Spearman rho(age, adult mortality) > 0
measured.uncertainty: 20 rising, 13 falling, 2 flat; 12 significantly rising and 6 significantly falling at p < 0.05

caveats: Verdict 'mixed' by the pre-registered rule (57% rising, between the 50% refute and 80% support thresholds): adult mortality rises with age in a majority of species but far from the 'great majority' that 'inevitable senescence' implies, and 13 of 35 species show falling adult mortality. This is the same direction as Jones et al. (2013) but weaker evidence, because matrix models have few age classes and noisy late-age estimates.
Sample is small (35 non-bird species, 20 of them mammals) and dominated by well-studied ungulates, carnivores and fishes; it is not a random sample of animal life histories.

Published age-classified matrices usually truncate age with a plus group, so the oldest ages, where senescence is strongest, are often missing; this biases the test against the claim. Conversely, class index is calendar age for most studies but not all.

The proved part of the claim (the formula for the age-specific force of selection) is not tested; only the biological corollary that mortality must rise with adult age. Class Aves (8 species) is held out and scorable later with 'analysis.py --exam'; the first run of the script, before the gate was added, printed the birds' fraction rising once and it was not used.

datasets.name: COMADRE Animal Matrix Database v4.26.4.0 (3548 matrix population models, 445 species)

tests.label: Kimura fixation probability of a mutant allele
tests.hypothesis: If a neutral allele's probability of eventual fixation equals its initial frequency, then in Buri's (1956) 107 replicate Drosophila populations, each started with the bw75 allele at frequency 0.5 in 16 flies, the lines that have reached fixation or loss by the last recorded generation should be split evenly between fixation of bw75 and loss of bw75.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: the 'fly' matrix in the CRAN package popgenr 0.2 (CC0; Laruson and Reed 2021), a 19 x 107 matrix of the number of bw75 allele copies (out of 32) in each replicate at each generation, transcribed from Buri (1956). At the last recorded generation, a line is 'fixed' if the count is 32 and 'lost' if the count is 0; m = fixed + lost, k = fixed. SUPPORTS if m >= 20 AND the two-sided exact binomial test of k against Binomial(m, 0.5) gives p > 0.05 AND |k/m - 0.5| < 0.15. Reported but not decisive: the mean bw75 frequency across all 107 lines at the last generation (predicted 0.5 under neutrality, since the expected frequency is constant under drift) and the number of fixed-or-lost lines.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the exact binomial test gives p < 0.01 (fixation significantly favours one allele) OR |k/m - 0.5| >= 0.25. MIXED otherwise (0.01 <= p <= 0.05, or 0.15 <= |k/m - 0.5| < 0.25). INCONCLUSIVE (underpowered) if m < 20; INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the package source cannot be downloaded.
tests.interpretation: The claim's neutral limit u(p) = p is tested at p = 0.5 with 32 gene copies per line. The selection-dependent form u(p) = (1 - exp(-4*Ne*s*p)) / (1 - exp(-4*Ne*s)) is not tested, because the selection coefficient of bw75 is not measured independently of these data (Buri himself reported a small heterozygote advantage in the series). A balanced split among fixed lines is the prediction of neutrality; a strong imbalance would show selection acting, which the claim's selective form would then describe but which this test could not quantify. Lines not yet fixed at the last generation are censored and do not enter k or m.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the CRAN tarball, extracts data/fly.RData and converts it with Rscript to derived/buri1956_fly.csv (committed, 1.7 KB). The object turned out to be a 20 x 33 generation-by-allele-count table (each row sums to 107 populations), not a 19 x 107 per-replicate matrix as the pre-registration assumed; the pre-registered quantities (number of populations fixed for bw75, k = 32 copies, and lost, k = 0, at the last recorded generation) are read directly from it. analysis.py applies the exact two-sided binomial test of fixed against Binomial(fixed + lost, 0.5) and reports the mean bw75 frequency and heterozygosity by generation, from whose decay an effective size is estimated for context.

measured.unit: fraction of fixed-or-lost populations fixed for bw75 at the last recorded generation (neutral prediction 0.5)
measured.n: 58 fixed-or-lost populations of 107 (28 fixed, 30 lost) after 19 generations

caveats: Only the neutral limit u(p) = p at p = 0.5 is tested; the selection-dependent formula is untested because s for bw75 is not independently known. The mean bw75 frequency drifted from 0.500 to 0.472 over 19 generations, a slight deficit that Buri attributed to weak selection; it is within what drift alone produces in 107 lines and does not change the fixed/lost balance.
The popgenr object is a transcription of Buri's published table; transcription accuracy was not checked against the 1956 paper (not open access).

Censoring: 49 of 107 lines were still segregating at the last generation; the test uses only lines that had resolved. Effective size from heterozygosity decay is about 8 (census 16), consistent with Buri's own estimate, so most fixations occurred before 4Ne generations had elapsed.

datasets.name: Buri (1956) 'Gene frequency in small populations of mutant Drosophila': allele-count distribution of bw75 in 107 replicate populations of 16 flies over 19 generations, as transcribed in the CRAN package popgenr 0.2 (object 'fly')

tests.label: Neutral equilibrium heterozygosity (Kimura-Crow)
tests.hypothesis: If neutral equilibrium heterozygosity H = theta/(1+theta) with theta = 4*Ne*mu holds and effective size scales with census size across species, then genome-wide nucleotide diversity (pi, the per-site heterozygosity) across metazoan species rises with census population size N: for pi << 1, H is approximately 4*Ne*mu, so log10(pi) should increase with log10(N) with a slope near 1 when mu and Ne/N are comparable across species, and the rank correlation between pi and N should be strongly positive.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: Buffalo (2021) combined_data.tsv from github.com/vsbuffalo/paradox_variation (commit b8f91d5, 2021-09-27), metazoan species (kingdom == Animalia) with a non-missing diversity value (pairwise nucleotide diversity, column 'diversity') and a non-missing census-size estimate (column 'log10_popsize', the posterior mean of log10 census size from the author's range x density model; if the file carries another census-size point estimate instead, the column actually used is recorded in 'method'). One row per species. SUPPORTS if Spearman rho(log10 pi, log10 N) > 0.5 with p < 0.001 AND the ordinary-least-squares slope of log10 pi on log10 N has a point estimate >= 0.3 with a 95% confidence interval that includes some value >= 0.5 (diversity rises at least about a third as fast as census size on a log scale, i.e. within a factor of about 3 of the law's slope of 1). AMENDMENT (2026-10-31, before any data were downloaded, at the request of the holdout thread): species of class Aves are excluded from the primary analysis and from all criteria above; bird rows are held out and only reported separately, unfitted, as a holdout check. The taxonomic class is taken from the file's own taxonomy columns.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the 95% confidence interval of the slope lies entirely below 0.25 (diversity rises less than a quarter as fast as census size on a log scale, so the law with N as the proxy for Ne is quantitatively wrong by orders of magnitude across the range of N: the Lewontin's-paradox pattern) OR rho <= 0. MIXED otherwise. INCONCLUSIVE (underpowered) if fewer than 50 species qualify; INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the file cannot be downloaded.
tests.interpretation: The claim is about effective population size Ne. Independent Ne estimates do not exist for most species, so census size N is used as the proxy, which is how Lewontin (1974) and Buffalo (2021) framed the paradox of variation. Mutation rates per site per generation vary by roughly an order of magnitude across metazoa and are not available per species here, so they are not included; a slope far below 1 therefore means that Ne is decoupled from N (by linked selection, demography or variation in mu), not that the within-model theorem is wrong. This is a test of the claim as the assessment proposed it ('regress genome-wide neutral diversity on estimates of Ne*mu across species'), with N standing in for Ne*mu.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads combined_data.tsv at the pinned commit. analysis.py keeps Animalia rows with a diversity value > 0 and a log10_popsize value (one row per species), drops the 13 class-Aves species (held out, never fitted), and on the remaining species computes Spearman rho between log10 diversity and log10 census size and an ordinary-least-squares regression of log10 diversity on log10 census size with a t-based 95% confidence interval on the slope. The decision rule is the pre-registered one.

measured.unit: OLS slope of log10(pi) on log10(census N); the law with Ne proportional to N predicts about 1
measured.n: 160 non-bird metazoan species (diversity sources: {'Leffler et al.': 90, 'Romiguier et al.': 58, 'Corbett-Detig et al.': 12})

caveats: Census size stands in for effective size and per-site mutation rate is not included, so the refutation is of the law as operationalized (diversity should track census size), which is exactly Lewontin's paradox: diversity does rise with N (rho about 0.5, p < 1e-10) but roughly ten times too slowly on a log scale, across 12 orders of magnitude of N.

Census sizes are model-based estimates (species range times a body-size-predicted density) with large uncertainty; measurement error in N attenuates the slope, but not by the factor of ten needed to rescue the law (Buffalo 2021 reaches the same conclusion with error-in-variables models).
Diversity estimates mix synonymous, non-coding and genome-wide measures from three collations, and are averaged where several entries exist for a species.

Class Aves (13 species) was excluded before fitting at the holdout thread's request and can be scored later with 'analysis.py --exam'. The first run of the script, before the gate was added, printed the birds' mean residual once; it was not used to change anything.
This is a cross-species pattern; it does not test the within-model derivation H = theta/(1+theta), which is a theorem.

datasets.name: Buffalo (2021) 'Why do species get a thin slice of pi?' combined species table: pairwise nucleotide diversity (collated from Leffler et al. 2012, Romiguier et al. 2014, Corbett-Detig et al. 2015) and census population size estimates (range x density model) for 300 metazoan species
datasets.license: not stated in the repository; the article is CC BY 4.0

tests.label: Genetic hitchhiking (selective sweep)
tests.hypothesis: If a favourable mutation's sweep removes variation at linked neutral sites, and more so where recombination is weaker relative to selection, then across windows of a human chromosome nucleotide diversity should be positively correlated with the local recombination rate.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 chromosome 22 genotype VCF (release 20130502, all 2504 samples) and the HapMap Phase II GRCh37 genetic map for chromosome 22. SNP filter: records with VT=SNP in INFO, biallelic (no MULTI_ALLELIC flag, single ALT), FILTER PASS. Windows: non-overlapping 200 kb windows starting at 16,000,000 bp (GRCh37) up to the last SNP. Diversity per window: pi = sum over SNPs of 2p(1-p) * 2n/(2n-1), with p the INFO AF value and 2n = 5008 chromosomes, divided by the window length (200,000 bp). Windows with fewer than 200 qualifying SNPs are excluded as unassessable (centromere-proximal or low-accessibility regions). Recombination rate per window: (map cM at window end minus map cM at window start) / 0.2 Mb, with cM linearly interpolated from the genetic map. SUPPORTS if Spearman rho(pi, recombination rate) across windows is >= 0.2 with two-sided p < 0.01.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if rho < 0 with p < 0.05 (diversity lower where recombination is higher) OR if |rho| < 0.1 with p > 0.05 and at least 100 windows (no detectable relationship). MIXED otherwise (0 <= rho < 0.2, or 0.01 <= p). INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if either file cannot be downloaded.
tests.interpretation: Maynard Smith and Haigh predicted that a sweep reduces heterozygosity at a linked neutral site by an amount that grows as recombination fraction over selection coefficient falls. The claim's assessment proposes the genome-wide version of the test used by Begun and Aquadro (1992): correlation between neutral diversity and local recombination rate. A positive correlation is also produced by background selection (Charlesworth et al. 1993), so a positive result supports the pattern the claim predicts but does not identify hitchhiking as the only cause; this is recorded as a caveat, not folded into the verdict. pi is computed from allele frequencies pooled across 26 populations; population structure inflates pooled pi roughly uniformly along the chromosome and does not create a correlation with recombination. All SNPs are used rather than only 'neutral' sites, which if anything weakens the expected correlation.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the chr22 VCF (205.6 MB) and the genetic-map archive. analysis.py streams the VCF, keeps PASS biallelic records with VT=SNP and without MULTI_ALLELIC, sums 2p(1-p)*2n/(2n-1) from the INFO AF value over non-overlapping 200 kb windows from 16.0 Mb, divides by window length to get pi, and takes the recombination rate per window from the linearly interpolated HapMap map; windows with fewer than 200 SNPs are excluded. Spearman and Pearson correlations between pi and rate across windows are computed and the pre-registered rule applied.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between per-window nucleotide diversity and recombination rate (cM/Mb), chr22, 200 kb windows

caveats: A positive diversity-recombination correlation is also produced by background selection (purifying selection removing linked neutral variation), so the result supports the pattern hitchhiking predicts but does not isolate sweeps as the cause; separating the two needs site-frequency or sweep-scan evidence.

Diversity is computed from allele frequencies pooled over all 26 populations; population structure inflates pi uniformly and does not create the correlation, but the absolute pi values are not a single-population estimate.

All SNPs are used, not only neutral sites; gene density and GC content covary with recombination in humans and could contribute to the correlation through mutation-rate variation. Windows with < 200 SNPs (none on chr22 above 16 Mb) would have been excluded.
One chromosome (22, about 35 Mb of assessable sequence) was tested, as pre-registered, to keep the download small; the pattern is well known genome-wide (Hellmann et al. 2003).

datasets.name: 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 integrated variant call set, chromosome 22 (release 20130502, 2504 samples, GRCh37)
datasets.license: open (Fort Lauderdale principles; IGSR terms of use)

datasets.name: HapMap Phase II LD-based recombination map lifted to GRCh37 (NCBI HapMap FTP, 2011-01 release)

tests.label: War of attrition ESS
tests.hypothesis: If display contests are wars of attrition in which each contestant draws a persistence time from an exponential distribution, then the durations of contests that end without escalation (the shorter of two independent exponential draws, which is itself exponential) should follow an exponential distribution.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: 'Vibrating aggression: spider males perform an unusual assessment strategy during contest displays', Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.bg79cnpjg, file fight.csv (male-male contests of the orb-web spider Trichonephila clavipes), restricted to contests recorded as not escalating to physical contact, using the contest duration column as given. SUPPORTS if n >= 20 AND a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of exponentiality with the rate estimated from the data (p-value calibrated by 10,000 parametric bootstrap replicates, i.e. a Lilliefors-type test) gives p > 0.05 AND the coefficient of variation of the durations lies in [0.7, 1.3].
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the bootstrap-calibrated test gives p < 0.01 AND the coefficient of variation lies outside [0.5, 1.5]. MIXED otherwise. INCONCLUSIVE (underpowered) if n < 20. INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if Dryad keeps blocking automated download (as of 2026-10-31 it serves a JavaScript proof-of-work challenge to scripted requests, which this project does not circumvent) and no manually downloaded copy with a recorded checksum is supplied.
tests.interpretation: The ESS of the symmetric war of attrition with cost linear in time is an exponential persistence time with mean equal to the resource value V; observed contest duration is the minimum of two such draws and so is exponential with mean V/2. Resource value is not varied in this dataset, so only the distributional prediction is tested, not the scaling of the mean with V. Durations are presumably recorded from the start of display with some time resolution, which can produce a floor; this is examined as a caveat if the data are obtained.
tests.method: fetch.py requested the file(s) by their Dryad file-stream URLs with a plain HTTP client and received HTTP 403 with a proof-of-work challenge page (the Dryad API download endpoint requires an account token). Per BEST_PRACTICES.md, sites that block automated requests are not circumvented, so no data were inspected and no analysis was run. fetch.py accepts a manually downloaded copy placed in data/ and records its checksum; the pre-registered analysis can then be run without changing the criteria.
caveats: The dataset exists and is public (CC0) but could not be fetched by script; a person with a browser can download it in seconds, after which this test is runnable as pre-registered.
Dryad's metadata API (which does not require a token) confirmed the file names and sizes; nothing about the data values was seen.

tests.label: Cold-blooded animals approach a maximal size only asymptotically
tests.hypothesis: If fishes approach a maximal size only asymptotically, then mean length at age in well-sampled wild fish populations keeps increasing, by ever smaller but still positive increments, through the oldest well-sampled ages, and an asymptotic growth model fits the length-at-age means better than a model in which length reaches a fixed maximum at a finite age and then stays there.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: ICES DATRAS North Sea IBTS (NS-IBTS) age records (CA record type), quarters 1 and 3, survey years 2000-2024, all species; length class converted to cm; records with a plus-group flag or missing age excluded. A species qualifies if it has at least 7 consecutive age classes starting at age 1, each with at least 50 aged fish (sum of CANoAtLngt); the included age range ends at the oldest class with at least 50 fish. For each species, mean length at age is computed (weighted by CANoAtLngt) and two 3-parameter models are fitted by weighted least squares (weights = number of fish): (i) asymptotic von Bertalanffy L = Linf (1 - exp(-K (a - t0))) with K > 0, and (ii) determinate quadratic-plateau L = Lmax - c (tc - a)^2 for a < tc, L = Lmax for a >= tc, with tc constrained to at most (oldest included age - 1) so that the model asserts a maximum actually reached inside the data. dAIC = AIC_det - AIC_VB (positive favours the asymptotic model). Late-age increments are the three increments of mean length between the last four included age classes. SUPPORTS if the asymptotic model is favoured (dAIC > 2) in at least two thirds of qualifying species AND at least 75% of all late-age increments pooled across species are positive. Requires at least 5 qualifying species; otherwise inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the determinate model is favoured (dAIC < -2) in at least half of the qualifying species, OR if at least half of the pooled late-age increments are zero or negative (growth has stopped at a reached maximum while fish are still well sampled). Anything between the supports and refutes conditions is 'mixed'. If the DATRAS download API is unreachable the verdict is inconclusive with reason data-unavailable.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'size never actually reaches, but only approaches asymptotically, a maximal limit' is read as a contrast between an asymptotic growth curve (increments decline toward zero but stay positive at every age reached) and determinate growth (a maximum reached at a finite age, with zero increments thereafter while the animals are alive). 'Size' is taken as body length, the quantity recorded in surveys. The test uses cross-sectional survey means of length at age rather than individual growth histories; this is a modern reinterpretation forced by the data (Thompson's own fish examples were also population means). Fitted asymptotic parameters are not themselves used as evidence of an asymptote, as one assessor warned; the evidence is the model comparison against an explicit reached-maximum alternative and the sign of the late-age increments.
tests.method: fetch.py requests one zip per survey year and quarter from the DATRAS Download API (50 files, 13.6 MB) and records their checksums. analysis.py pools all records, converts length classes to cm, drops plus-group and unaged records, and computes the CANoAtLngt-weighted mean length at age per species. For the 11 species with at least 7 consecutive age classes from age 1 each holding >= 50 aged fish, it fits by weighted least squares a 3-parameter von Bertalanffy curve and a 3-parameter quadratic-plateau curve whose maximum is reached at least one age class before the oldest included age, and compares them by AIC; it also records the sign of the three increments between the last four included age classes.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying species in which the asymptotic model is favoured by dAIC > 2 (pre-registered threshold 2/3); fraction of late-age increments positive = 0.758 (threshold 0.75)
measured.n: 11 species, 33 late-age increments, 1111408 aged fish from 986385 CA rows
measured.uncertainty: species-level counts: 7 of 11 favour the asymptotic model, 2 of 11 (Merlangius merlangus, Microstomus kitt) favour the reached-maximum model, 2 indeterminate (|dAIC| <= 2); 25 of 33 late increments > 0

caveats: The pre-registered supports condition was narrowly missed: 7/11 = 0.636 species favour the asymptotic model against the required 2/3, while the late-increment condition (0.758 >= 0.75) was met. The result is therefore 'mixed' by rule, although most of the evidence points toward protracted growth.

In the two species where the reached-maximum model wins (whiting, lemon sole) mean length at age actually declines over the oldest ages, which neither model predicts for individual growth; the most likely cause is size-selective (fishing) mortality removing the faster growers (Lee's phenomenon) and ageing error, not cessation of growth. This biases the test against the claim.

Cross-sectional survey means pool cohorts and years (2000-2024, Q1 and Q3) and so mix cohort effects with age effects; the oldest age classes are sparsely sampled (>= 50 fish required) and trawl gear under-samples the largest fish.

The determinate alternative had to be given a specific functional form (quadratic rise to a plateau); a different plateau model could change individual dAIC values. Model selection used AIC on 7-18 age-class means, not individual-level likelihoods.

Scope: North Sea marine teleosts only (11 species); Thompson's scope was cold-blooded animals in general. For saithe and cod the oldest well-sampled fish are at only 48-65% of the fitted Linf, i.e. the data do not reach the asymptotic region at all.

DATRAS is a live database; the API extract is reproducible only to the extent that ICES does not revise the 2000-2024 records. The 50 file checksums of the extract used are in derived/datras_file_manifest.json and in this file.
DATRAS 'Species' names are taken as delivered (AphiaID-based) and no taxonomic harmonisation was done.

tests.label: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex
tests.hypothesis: If the sutural line of a turreted shell such as Turritella is a geodesic of the shell's enveloping right cone, then the number of whorls the suture makes cannot exceed the number of turns a conical geodesic can make: a geodesic on a right cone of apical angle alpha develops into a straight line on a sector of angle 2*pi*sin(alpha/2), sweeps at most pi of that sector, and therefore turns at most N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) times in total (and only half of that while approaching the apex). Measured whorl counts of Turritella shells must therefore satisfy N_obs <= N_geo.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. From published per-specimen measurements of Turritellidae giving both the apical angle alpha and the total whorl number N_obs (Pandita et al. 2013, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6, 50 specimens of 5 species), compute N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) and the ratio R = N_obs / N_geo for every specimen with both values. SUPPORTS if at least 90% of specimens have R <= 1 (whorl count within the geodesic bound).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if at least 90% of specimens have R > 1, i.e. the suture coils more times than any geodesic of the enveloping cone can, so the sutural line cannot be a conical geodesic. Between 10% and 90% is 'mixed'. If the tables cannot be retrieved or parsed, inconclusive with reason data-unavailable. The claim's first part (coils tighten toward the apex) is shared by a geodesic and by the logarithmic helico-spiral and is not discriminating; the verdict rests on the identification of the suture with a geodesic.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'spiral geodetic' on a right cone is taken literally (a curve of zero geodesic curvature on the enveloping cone), and 'the sutural line ... such as Turritella ... is a geodetic of this kind' as the claim that the suture follows such a curve. The enveloping surface of a turritellid is close to a right circular cone whose apical angle is the measured alpha. The test uses only two gross measurements per shell, apical angle and whorl number, because the geodesic bound on the number of turns depends on nothing else. Whorl counts in the source include the early (protoconch/juvenile) whorls, where the cone approximation is roughest; the result is checked for sensitivity by also subtracting two whorls from every count.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the article PDF, records its SHA-256 and transcribes Tables 2-6 with pdfplumber into derived/pandita2013_turritellidae.csv (49 rows; all published ratio columns Wang:L and Wsut:L were recomputed from the transcribed measurements and agree, confirming the transcription). analysis.py computes for each of the 34 specimens with both apical angle and whorl number the maximum number of turns of a geodesic on a right cone of that apical angle, N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)), the ratio R = whorls/N_geo, the same ratio after subtracting two whorls (allowance for the protoconch/early whorls), and the apical angle that would have been needed for the observed whorl count to fit a geodesic.

measured.unit: median ratio of observed whorl number to the maximum number of turns a conical geodesic can make (R = N_obs / N_geo); R > 1 is impossible for a geodesic
measured.uncertainty: R ranges from 1.63 to 3.39 across all 34 specimens (4 species); every specimen exceeds the bound

caveats: The test refutes the identification of the suture with a geodesic of the enveloping right cone; it does not test Thompson's purely geometric statement that a conical geodesic coils more closely toward the apex (true) nor whether the suture is locally geodesic-like over a fraction of a whorl.

The bound assumes the shell envelope is a right circular cone, which is what Thompson states; real turritellid envelopes are slightly convex or concave, but the Clairaut relation on any such surface of revolution still forbids a geodesic from winding many times toward a narrowing apex unless the sides are almost parallel.

Specimens are Neogene fossils from West Java, not the type species Turritella terebra; fossil apices are often incomplete, so whorl counts are if anything underestimates, which makes the test conservative. Apical angles are the authors' gross measurements to 0.5 degree.
Whorl counts include early whorls where the cone approximation is roughest; subtracting two whorls from every count leaves all 34 specimens above the bound.
The published tables list 50 specimens in the text but 49 rows were present (Table 6 lacks a specimen 5B); 15 rows lack an apical angle and were excluded.
Transcription from the PDF needs pdfplumber (not in the standard tool list); the transcribed table is committed so analysis.py runs with pandas and numpy only.

datasets.name: Pandita, Zaim, Aswan & Rizal (2013) Relationship of Biometrical Aspect of Turritellidae with Geochronological Aspect in West Java, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6 (biometric measurements of 49 turritellid specimens from five Neogene localities)

tests.label: Each increment of a spirally grown structure is a gnomon to the whole before it
tests.hypothesis: If every increment of a spirally grown shell is a gnomon to the whole structure before it (the enlarged whole stays similar to itself), then a molluscan shell is geometrically self-similar through growth: dimensionless shape indices of the conch measured at successive diameters along one specimen's ontogeny (conch width index CWI = ww/dm, umbilical width index UWI = uw/dm, whorl expansion rate WER) stay constant, apart from measurement noise, from the end of the embryonic shell to maturity.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: Walton & Korn (2018) ontogenetic conch-parameter series for 177 Devonian-Jurassic ammonoid species (Dryad 10.5061/dryad.c17p8), measured on median cross-sections at successive diameters dm. For each species keep the post-embryonic points (dm >= 2 mm) and require at least 4 points spanning at least a fourfold range of dm. For each retained index compute the log-range D = max ln(index) - min ln(index) over the series. A species is 'gnomonic' if D <= ln(1.25) (at most 25% change) for CWI, UWI and WER alike; 'allometric' if D >= ln(1.5) (at least 50% change) for at least one index; otherwise intermediate. SUPPORTS if at least two thirds of the qualifying species are gnomonic. As a secondary descriptor, the fraction of species whose indices show a monotonic trend with ln dm (|Spearman rho| >= 0.7, p < 0.05, for at least one index) is reported; it does not enter the verdict.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if at least two thirds of the qualifying species are allometric (at least one shape index changes by 50% or more over post-embryonic growth, so successive increments are not gnomons of the pre-existing conch). Otherwise 'mixed'. Fewer than 30 qualifying species: inconclusive (underpowered). File unobtainable: inconclusive, data-unavailable.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's gnomon is 'an addition that leaves the enlarged whole similar to what it was before'; for a coiled conch, continued similarity means that the ratios describing its shape are unchanged by growth, which is exactly what constant CWI, UWI and WER along an ontogenetic trajectory express (constant WER is the constant spiral angle; constant CWI and UWI fix the whorl-section proportions and the umbilicus). Ammonoid conchs are molluscan shells, within the stated scope. The embryonic ammonitella (dm below about 1-2 mm) formed inside the egg rather than by the accretion Thompson describes, so points below 2 mm are excluded. Thresholds of 25% and 50% are chosen before analysis to separate measurement noise in cross-sections from genuine shape change; the measurement protocol (Korn 2010) reports typical errors of a few percent.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the Dryad version zip and records its SHA-256. analysis.py reshapes the four parameter sheets to one long table (species, half-whorl, dm, CWI, UWI, WER), keeps post-embryonic points (dm >= 2 mm) and the 179 series with >= 4 points spanning >= 4x in diameter, and for each index computes the log-range over the series (percent change), a Spearman correlation with ln dm, and classifies each series as gnomonic (all three indices change <= 25%), allometric (any index changes >= 50%) or intermediate. Sensitivity runs use dm >= 5 mm and drop UWI.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying ammonoid series in which at least one conch shape index changes by >= 50% over post-embryonic growth (pre-registered refutes threshold 2/3); fraction gnomonic = 0.006 (supports threshold 2/3)
measured.uncertainty: 168 allometric, 10 intermediate, 1 gnomonic (Eurites permutus); 93.9% of series show a monotonic trend (|Spearman rho| >= 0.7, p < 0.05) in at least one index

caveats: The refutation is carried almost entirely by the umbilical width index: UWI changes by >= 50% in 92% of series (median change 204%), whereas the whorl expansion rate, which encodes the spiral angle, stays within 25% in 80% of series (median change 17%). The spiral itself is therefore close to logarithmic (gnomonic in Thompson's sense), while the whorl section and the degree of involution change through growth, so the enlarged conch is not similar to its earlier self. Dropping UWI, only 34% of series (27% at dm >= 5 mm) are allometric and the pre-registered rule would give 'mixed'.

Walton & Korn chose their 177 species to study pachyconic and globular ammonoids with phased ontogenies, so the sample is probably enriched in species with strong ontogenetic shape change relative to ammonoids at large.

UWI is the noisiest index at small diameters (small umbilical widths); the 2 mm cut-off and the requirement of a monotonic trend (met by 94% of series) limit but do not remove this effect; at dm >= 5 mm the allometric fraction is still 84%.

Scope: Palaeozoic-Jurassic ammonoid conchs only; Thompson's gnomon claim also covers gastropod and bivalve shells, opercula, foraminiferal chambers, horns and tusks, which were not tested. The 25% and 50% thresholds are pre-registered conventions, not derived from Thompson.

Thompson himself notes elsewhere (ch. XI, changes of spiral angle with age) that some ammonoids change their spiral angle during growth; this test shows that even where the spiral angle is nearly constant, the conch shape generally is not.

datasets.name: Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn 2018, Palaeontology 61, doi:10.1111/pala.12308)
datasets.version: Dryad version id 7242 = dataset version 1 (published 2018-05-16), the only publicly listed version

tests.label: Aquatic mammals lack the tall withers and haunch spines of land quadrupeds
tests.hypothesis: If buoyancy has removed the tall arched neural spines over the withers and haunches, then secondarily aquatic mammals (pinnipeds, cetaceans) should show no anterior-thoracic ('withers') peak of relative neural-spine height along the thoracolumbar column, and their anterior-thoracic spines should be relatively shorter than those of terrestrial quadrupeds; the haunch (posterior lumbar) spines should likewise not be elevated.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Per vertebra, relative spine height h = (neural spine apex to centrum reference distance) / cranial centrum height. Per species: W = mean h over T1-T4 ('withers'); P = mean h over the posterior thoracics T10-T13 (terrestrial trough region); WI = W/P ('withers index'); HI = mean h over the last three lumbars / P ('haunch index'). Test A (Carnivora landmark data, Figueirido et al. 2021): SUPPORTS-component if every pinniped species has W below the 25th percentile of terrestrial carnivoran W and one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests give p < 0.05 for pinnipeds < terrestrial on both W and WI. Test B (cetacean linear data, Gillet et al. 2019, h = Lnp/Hc; W over the first three thoracics, P over the last three thoracics, WI = W/P): SUPPORTS-component if the median cetacean WI <= 1 and at least 80% of cetacean species have WI below the minimum WI of the terrestrial carnivorans from Test A. Overall verdict 'supports' only if both components support.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. Because the claim says the spines have 'entirely disappeared' in 'all aquatic mammals', a single aquatic group retaining a terrestrial-grade withers refutes it. REFUTES if (A) any pinniped species has W >= the terrestrial carnivoran median W, or (B) at least 20% of cetacean species have WI >= the terrestrial carnivoran median WI (an anterior-thoracic peak of terrestrial proportions). If neither the supports nor the refutes conditions are met, the verdict is 'mixed'. If a required measurement (spine landmarks, Lnp or Hc) is missing from the files, that component is 'inconclusive / data-unavailable'.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'high arched vertebral spines over the withers' are read as a regional peak of tall neural spines in the anterior thoracic vertebrae, and the 'corresponding structures over the hind-limbs' as tall posterior lumbar (haunch) spines; 'disappeared' is read as absence of that peak relative to the posterior-thoracic trough and relative shortness compared with terrestrial relatives. Spine height is normalised by centrum height within each vertebra so that it is size-free. Pinnipeds are compared with terrestrial members of the same order (Carnivora), as the claim requires ('terrestrial relatives'). Cetaceans have no terrestrial comparator in the same dataset, so for them only the within-column profile (withers index) is compared with the terrestrial carnivoran reference distribution. Sirenians and the bird-pelvis part of the claim are not tested: no public tabular morphometric dataset covering them was identified before pre-registration; this is recorded as a caveat and the verdict is restricted to pinnipeds and cetaceans. In the landmark data the 'spine apex to centrum reference' distance is from the most distal spinous-process landmark to the centroid of the four cranial centrum-face landmarks (so it includes the neural arch), and centrum height is the largest diameter of that face; in the cetacean data it is the authors' neural-spine height (Lnp) over centrum height (Hc). Because the two definitions differ, absolute h values are not compared across datasets, only the within-column ratio WI.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads both Dryad version zips and records their SHA-256. analysis.py parses the IDAV landmark files, computes for each thoracic and lumbar vertebra the distance from the most distal spinous-process landmark to the centroid of the cranial centrum-face landmarks divided by the largest diameter of that face (h), averages h over T1-T4 (W), T10-T13 (P) and the last three lumbars, and forms WI = W/P and HI per specimen and then per species. Pinnipeds (n = 2 species) are compared with the 40 terrestrial carnivorans (otters and mink excluded from the reference set; sensitivity run includes them) by exact one-sided Mann-Whitney U tests and by position relative to the terrestrial quantiles. For the cetaceans, h = Lnp/Hc is computed for all 8722 measured vertebrae, WI = mean h of the first three thoracics / mean h of the last three thoracics per specimen, averaged per species, and compared with the terrestrial carnivoran WI distribution.

measured.unit: withers index WI (mean of the two pinniped species); terrestrial carnivoran WI min 1.238, median 1.910
measured.n: 45 carnivoran species (951 vertebrae) incl. 2 pinnipeds; 74 cetacean species (204 specimens, 8722 vertebrae)
measured.uncertainty: exact one-sided Mann-Whitney U, pinnipeds < terrestrial: W p = 0.0023, WI p = 0.0012 (n = 2 vs 40; smallest attainable p = 0.0012)

caveats: Only two pinniped species (one phocid, one otariid) are in the carnivoran dataset; sirenians are absent from both datasets, and the bird-pelvis half of the claim was not tested at all. The verdict therefore covers pinnipeds and cetaceans only, not Thompson's 'all aquatic mammals'.

The 'haunch' part is not discriminating in Carnivora: terrestrial carnivorans themselves show no posterior-lumbar spine peak (median HI 0.80 < 1), and pinniped HI falls inside the terrestrial range (p = 0.77). Thompson's haunch spines refer mainly to ungulates, for which no comparable public data were used.

Pinniped anterior-thoracic spines are reduced (W 2.3-2.7 vs terrestrial 2.6-5.3) and the withers peak is absent (WI about 1.0), but the spines have not literally 'entirely disappeared'; Otaria byronia's W lies above the lowest terrestrial species (Martes foina).

Relative spine height from landmarks includes the neural arch and depends on where the authors placed the spinous-process landmarks; the cetacean values come from a different measurement protocol, so only the within-column ratio WI is compared across datasets.
No phylogenetic comparative model was fitted (two pinniped species cannot support one); the Mann-Whitney test treats species as independent.

Semi-aquatic carnivorans (otters, mink) retain a terrestrial-grade withers index (1.6-1.7), consistent with Thompson's restriction to animals whose weight is carried by water, but they were excluded from the terrestrial reference set by a decision taken before analysis; including them does not change the result.
Gillet et al. label 74 species where the paper reports 73 (one specimen label is spelled 'Feresa_attenuta'); species means were taken as labelled.
